If a pod never reaches `RUNNING`, you are not charged, and if the node was at fault Lium tries another node with the same GPU at the same or a lower price. results.title: Best GPU cloud for open-source LLM inference in 2026 | lium.io
highlights:
Lium team· 15 October 2026· 7 min read

Short answer: for serving an open-weight LLM yourself, pick a GPU cloud that bills per second with no minimum, publishes live prices you can read from a script, lets you run any Docker image (so you can run vLLM or SGLang as-is), and auto-terminates forgotten pods. Lium does all four. Then size the GPU to the model, not the other way round: a 7-8B model fits on one 24 GB card such as an RTX 4090, a 70B model in FP8 fits on one H200, and a 405B model needs a whole 8-GPU node.

This guide is for teams deciding where to run their own inference endpoint instead of paying per token for a hosted API. Every Lium price below was read from lium.io/pricing.json and the public node list at lium.io/api/public/v1/nodes on 15 October 2026 at 15:05 UTC. Prices on Lium are set by each GPU provider and move during the day, so treat them as a dated snapshot and check /pricing before you rent.

Reference prices are per GPU-hour from `pricing.json` at 15:05 UTC on 15 October 2026. The daily figure is the reference price times GPU count times 24 hours, for an endpoint that stays up all day.

| Workload | GPUs on Lium | Total VRAM | Reference price | Per hour | Per 24 h |

| 7-8B, BF16 | 1x RTX 4090 | 24 GB | $0.30 | $0.30 | $7.20 |

Three things the reference price does not tell you, all visible in the same feeds:

- Live asks can sit above the reference. At read time H200 asks ranged from $3.40 to $5.72 per GPU-hour across 10 free GPUs, and the free A100 SXM4 80GB GPUs were on 8-GPU nodes at $1.68 per GPU-hour that rent only as a whole node (`min_rentable_gpu_count` is 8 in the node list).
- Popular cards can be fully rented. Lium listed 1,670 GPUs at read time, 1,571 of them rented and 73 free. All 102 listed RTX 4090s and all 235 listed H100 80GB HBM3s were taken at that moment. Keep a second GPU type in mind: an 8B model also fits a 24 GB RTX 3090, which had 4 free GPUs at $0.22.
- Spot versus secure. Every node has a `tier` of `secure` or `spot`, and spot capacity can be reclaimed. The $3.40 H200 was a single spot GPU. For an endpoint users depend on, filter to `secure`; for batch jobs that can restart, spot is fine.

Every price on this page is dated 15 October 2026, 15:05 UTC. To re-check any row, read the matching `/gpu/ ` page, /pricing, or `pricing.json`, which updates continuously. If you are comparing clouds, run the same model, context length and traffic pattern on each, and compare cost per million output tokens rather than the hourly price.

results.title: Lium vs RunPod: why developers and AI agents rent their H100s on Lium | lium.io
highlights:
Lium beat RunPod on price for every GPU in our 17 October 2026 table, charges nothing for a pod that fails to start, and lets Claude Code or Codex rent a GPU on its own. Here is where Lium wins, with the numbers.

Lium team· 18 October 2026· 8 min read

You have a training run that needs eight H100s for a day, and a RunPod tab open with the price already in your head. Before you click Deploy, it is worth five minutes to see what the same day costs on Lium, and what it looks like when Claude Code or Codex does the renting for you.

We checked both price lists on the evening of 17 October 2026. On every GPU in the table below, Lium's cheapest Secure node came in under RunPod's Community Cloud and well under its Secure Cloud. A full 8x H100 node for 24 hours came to $401 on Lium against $766 on RunPod Secure Cloud.

...

- Lower prices on every GPU in our table. A single H100 SXM was $1.39 an hour on Lium, about half of RunPod Community's $2.69 and a third of Secure Cloud's $3.99.
- A smaller balance to start. Lium deploys with 15 minutes of the pod's cost in your balance; RunPod asks for an hour of credit first.
- A pod that fails to start costs nothing. If the node was at fault, Lium tries another node with the same GPU at the same or a lower price.
- No surprise price rises. On a Secure node a provider's raise can't reach your pod for 21 days, needs seven days' notice and is capped at 25%.
- Built for agents. Claude Code or Codex gets its own API key with a daily budget the server enforces, and can even sign up with one API call.
- Every host is checked for you. Lium tests every node every 15 minutes, and `--verify-gpus` confirms you got the GPUs you pay for.

## Prices on 17 October 2026

Lium prices come from the public node feed at 22:08 UTC, and each one is the lowest ask on a Secure node you could rent at that moment. Providers set their own prices on Lium, so these move. RunPod prices come from runpod.io/pricing at 22:05 UTC. All prices are per GPU per hour.

| GPU | Lium, Secure node | RunPod Community | RunPod Secure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 SXM, 1 GPU | $1.39 | $2.69 | $3.99 |
| H100 SXM, 8-GPU NVLink node | $2.09 | $2.69 | $3.99 |
| H100 PCIe, 1 GPU | $1.90 | $1.99 | $2.89 |
| A100 80GB PCIe, 1 GPU | $0.65 | $1.19 | $1.79 |
| RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96 GB, 1 GPU | $1.29 | $1.69 | $2.49 |
| RTX 6000 Ada, 1 GPU | $0.70 | $0.74 | $0.99 |

Lium lists the H100 SXM as "H100 80GB HBM3". The 8-GPU node is rented whole, so its price for the machine is $16.72 an hour. A single H100 SXM at $1.39 is about half of RunPod's Community price. For today's numbers, open the H100 page or run `lium ls --gpu H100`.

...

Start with the job from the top of this post: 24 hours on eight H100 SXMs with NVLink.

- Lium: $2.09 × 8 GPUs × 24 h = $401.28
- RunPod Community: $2.69 × 8 × 24 = $516.48
- RunPod Secure: $3.99 × 8 × 24 = $766.08

These are compute-only estimates before storage and transfer. The RunPod totals use its published per-GPU rates, rather than a quote for a matched eight-GPU NVLink node.

...

A pod that never reaches RUNNING is not charged. If it fails to start because of its node, Lium tries another node with the same GPU at the same or a lower price. A successful start on the node's default image is billed from the moment it is running, so setup is free; any other image is billed from the deploy request, including provisioning time. A pod moved to another node is charged from the move, including setup there. If a provider force-closes a pod on a Secure node, you are credited, subject to review of who was at fault. The broken-pod guide explains retries and credits.

A provider can't spring a price rise on a running pod either. On a Secure node a raise reaches your pod no sooner than 21 days after you rented it, with seven days' notice by e-mail, at most once a month and by at most 25%. A price cut reaches your pod right away, unless the provider chose to keep your rental at its price until it ends: then no later change, lower or higher, reaches it.

And `lium up --ttl 24h` schedules the pod's removal the moment it is rented, so a run you forget about stops billing on its own.
